key_verses.sanskrit: सुनु खगेस नहिं कछु रिषि दूषन। उर प्रेरक रघुबंस बिभूषन॥ कृपासिंधु मुनि मति करि भोरी। लीन्ही प्रेम परिच्छा मोरी ॥
key_verses.gist: Listen, lord of birds: there was no fault in the sage. Ram, who moves the heart, dulled the sage's mind and tested my love.

key_verses.sanskrit: भगति पच्छ हठ करि रहेउँ दीन्हि महारिषि साप। मुनि दुर्लभ बर पायउँ देखहु भजन प्रताप ॥
key_verses.gist: I held fast to the side of devotion and the great sage cursed me; I gained a boon rare even for sages. See the power of bhajan.

content_hook: He was cursed into a crow by a great sage, bowed, and flew off happy. That crow told the Ramayana to Garuda.

title: Garuda asks what the diseases of the mind are, and is given a diagnosis and a cure
source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 117 to 118 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
the_moment: After hearing the whole story, Garuda asks his last questions. The seventh: explain the diseases of the mind (manas rog), by which everyone suffers.
what_they_did: Kakbhushundi answers like a physician. Delusion is the root of all diseases; from it come many pains. Desire is wind, greed is phlegm, anger is bile that burns the chest; when the three combine you get delirium. Possessiveness is ringworm, envy is itch, swings of joy and grief are throat disease, burning at others' happiness is consumption, malice is leprosy. Ego is a painful tumour, hypocrisy, deceit, arrogance and vanity are the guinea worm, craving is dropsy, the three cravings (for sons, wealth and fame) are recurring fever, jealousy and lack of discernment are two fevers. Everyone is a patient; knowing the diseases weakens them but does not destroy them.
the_turn: The cure: by Ram's grace, if this combination forms: trust in the word of the true guru as physician; the restraint of not hoping for sense objects; devotion to Ram as the life-restoring herb; faith-filled understanding as the vehicle to take it in. And the signs of recovery: dispassion grows strong in the heart, the hunger for good understanding grows daily, and the weakness of craving for sense objects goes.
outcome: Garuda is fully satisfied and bows again and again.
whole_arc_note: The diagnosis is sobering (everyone is ill, knowing is not curing), and the remedy is specific and devotional. Do not present it as self-help; the text says grace, a teacher, restraint and devotion together.
teaching: Delusion is the root of the mind's diseases; grace, a true teacher, restraint and devotion are the cure.
framework: Manas Rog (Uttar Kand): root = moha (delusion). kama = vata (wind), lobha = kapha (phlegm), krodha = pitta (bile); all three together = sannipata (delirium). mamata = ringworm; irsha = itch; harsha-vishada = throat disease; burning at others' joy = consumption; dushtata = leprosy; ahankara = tumour; dambha, kapat, mada, mana = guinea worm; trishna = dropsy; three eshanas = recurring fever; matsara and aviveka = two fevers. Remedy: Ram's grace + sadguru as physician (trust his word) + sanyam (no hoping for sense objects) as diet + Raghupati-bhakti as sanjivani herb + shraddha as the honey it is taken in. Signs of health: vairagya grows, hunger for sumati grows, craving weakens.
modern_parallels: I can name every one of my patterns, my therapist and I have mapped them. Naming them has not made them go.
Envy is eating me. I want to know what is actually wrong with me, not just how to cope.
My anger, my greed for more, my restless wanting: they feed each other.
How do I know I am getting better? What does a healthy mind actually feel like?

key_verses.sanskrit: मानस रोग कहहु समुझाई। तुम्ह सर्बग्य कृपा अधिकाई॥ तात सुनहु सादर अति प्रीती। मैं संछेप कहउँ यह नीती ॥
key_verses.gist: Explain the diseases of the mind; you are all-knowing and most gracious. Listen, son, with care and love: I will tell it briefly.

key_verses.sanskrit: मोह सकल ब्याधिन्ह कर मूला। तिन्ह ते पुनि उपजहिं बहु सूला॥ काम बात कफ लोभ अपारा। क्रोध पित्त नित छाती जारा ॥
key_verses.gist: Delusion is the root of all diseases; from them arise many pains. Desire is wind, boundless greed is phlegm, anger is bile that keeps the chest burning.

key_verses.sanskrit: अहंकार अति दुखद डमरुआ। दंभ कपट मद मान नेहरुआ॥ तृस्ना उदरबृद्धि अति भारी। त्रिबिधि ईषना तरुन तिजारी ॥
key_verses.gist: Ego is a most painful tumour; hypocrisy, deceit, arrogance and vanity the guinea worm; craving the great dropsy; the three cravings a recurring fever.

key_verses.sanskrit: राम कृपाँ नासहिं सब रोगा। जौं एहि भाँति बनै संजोगा॥ सदगुर बैद बचन बिस्वासा। संजम यह न बिषय कै आसा ॥
key_verses.gist: By Ram's grace all diseases perish, if this combination forms: trust in the word of the true guru as physician, and restraint, no hope for sense objects.

key_verses.sanskrit: रघुपति भगति सजीवन मूरी। अनूपान श्रद्धा मति पूरी॥ एहि बिधि भलेहिं सो रोग नसाहीं। नाहिं त जतन कोटि नहिं जाहीं ॥
key_verses.gist: Devotion to Raghupati is the life-giving herb; understanding full of faith is the medium it is taken in.

key_verses.sanskrit: जानिअ तब मन बिरुज गोसाँई। जब उर बल बिराग अधिकाई॥ सुमति छुधा बाढ़इ नित नई। बिषय आस दुर्बलता गई ॥
key_verses.gist: Know the mind is healed, sir, when dispassion grows strong in the heart, the hunger for good understanding grows daily, and the weakness of sense craving is gone.

content_hook: Tulsidas wrote a full medical chart of the mind 400 years ago: anger is bile, greed is phlegm, desire is wind.

title: Kakbhushundi explains why the lamp of knowledge goes out and the gem of devotion does not
source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand, dohas 114 to 116 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
the_moment: Garuda asks the difference between knowledge and devotion. Kakbhushundi, who has walked both paths and was cursed for preferring one, answers with an image Garuda can hold.
what_they_did: He describes knowledge as a lamp lit with enormous labour: the cow of faith, the milk of good practice, churned, made into ghee, a wick of steady practice, finally the flame of 'I am That'. Then maya sends riddhis and siddhis to tempt the intellect, and the gods of the senses open the windows of the heart, and the wind blows the lamp out. Knowledge is hard to speak of, hard to understand, and hard to practise; walking it is walking a sword's edge.
the_turn: Then the contrast: devotion to Ram is a wish-fulfilling gem. It shines day and night by its own light, needing no lamp, ghee or wick. Its light destroys the darkness of ignorance, moths like pride cannot approach it, and the winds of greed cannot shake it. One in whose heart it dwells has not a trace of sorrow even in dreams.
outcome: Garuda's doubt about the paths is resolved, though Kakbhushundi adds that the gem, though present in the world, is found only by Ram's grace, with the help of the good.
whole_arc_note: Kakbhushundi does not dismiss knowledge; he calls it true and describes it with respect. The contrast is about fragility and labour, not worth. Present it as the Manas's own position, a devotional one.
teaching: Knowledge is a lamp the winds can put out; devotion is a gem that shines by itself.
framework: Jnana-deepak (Uttar Kand): sattvik shraddha (cow) -> good conduct (milk) -> churned by non-attachment -> ghee of self-restraint -> lamp of steady mind, wick of the three states -> flame of 'so'ham asmi'. Threats: riddhi-siddhi temptations, the senses opening the windows, the wind of sense desire. Bhakti-mani: self-luminous, needs no fuel, is not shaken by greed's wind, keeps moths of mada away; found by Ram's grace and satsang.
modern_parallels: I have read every book on meditation and still lose my calm the moment someone cuts me off in traffic.
My practice took years to build and one bad month blew it out.
I envy my grandmother's simple faith. Nothing seems to shake it.
Which is better, understanding or devotion? I keep going back and forth.

key_verses.sanskrit: सोहमस्मि इति बृत्ति अखंडा। दीप सिखा सोइ परम प्रचंडा॥ आतम अनुभव सुख सुप्रकासा। तब भव मूल भेद भ्रम नासा ॥
key_verses.gist: 'I am That': the unbroken thought is the lamp's flame, supremely bright.

key_verses.sanskrit: जब सो प्रभंजन उर गृहँ जाई। तबहिं दीप बिग्यान बुझाई॥ ग्रंथि न छूटि मिटा सो प्रकासा। बुद्धि बिकल भइ बिषय बतासा ॥
key_verses.gist: As soon as that fierce wind enters the house of the heart, the lamp of knowledge goes out.

key_verses.sanskrit: ग्यान पंथ कृपान कै धारा। परत खगेस होइ नहिं बारा॥ जो निर्बिघ्न पंथ निर्बहई। सो कैवल्य परम पद लहई ॥
key_verses.gist: The path of knowledge is a sword's edge; falling from it takes no time, lord of birds.

key_verses.sanskrit: कहेउँ ग्यान सिद्धांत बुझाई। सुनहु भगति मनि कै प्रभुताई॥ राम भगति चिंतामनि सुंदर। बसइ गरुड़ जाके उर अंतर ॥
key_verses.gist: I have explained the doctrine of knowledge; now hear the power of the gem of devotion. Devotion to Ram is a beautiful wish-fulfilling gem.

key_verses.sanskrit: राम भगति मनि उर बस जाकें। दुख लवलेस न सपनेहुँ ताकें॥ चतुर सिरोमनि तेइ जग माहीं। जे मनि लागि सुजतन कराहीं ॥
key_verses.gist: One in whose heart the gem of devotion to Ram dwells has not a trace of sorrow even in dreams.

content_hook: Knowledge is a lamp: years to light, one gust to blow out. Devotion is a gem: it shines on its own.

title: Tara weeps over her husband, and the one who killed him consoles her
source_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand, dohas 11 to 12 (corpus and library numbering; Gita Press counts can run a few dohas higher)
the_moment: Bali lies dead by Ram's arrow. His wife Tara, who had begged him not to go out to fight, runs to the field, her hair loose, and falls over his body in many kinds of lament.
what_they_did: Ram sees her distress and gives her knowledge that removes her delusion: the body is made of the five elements, earth, water, fire, sky and air; that body lies here before you, and the soul is eternal. For whom do you weep? She understands, falls at his feet and asks for devotion.
the_turn: Ram says it himself, gently and directly, to the woman whose husband he has just killed, and Tulsi says it was given by grace: dinha gyana hari linhi maya.
outcome: Tara receives knowledge and devotion; Sugriva is crowned and Angad made heir.
whole_arc_note: Note who speaks and how: it is grace given in person, at the right moment, and the text says it removed maya rather than merely argued. Using this verse to tell a fresh griever 'why are you crying' would invert it. Her earlier warning to Bali, which he dismissed, is part of the arc.
teaching: The body is made of elements and lies before us; the one we love is not only that.
modern_parallels: My husband died suddenly and I keep looking at his body in my mind.
I warned him not to drive that night.
Someone said to me, 'the soul does not die'. It helped only because she said it holding my hand.
I want to understand what actually left when he died.

key_verses.sanskrit: तारा बिकल देखि रघुराया। दीन्ह ग्यान हरि लीन्ही माया॥ छिति जल पावक गगन समीरा। पंच रचित अति अधम सरीरा ॥
key_verses.gist: Seeing Tara distraught, Raghurai gave her knowledge and took away her delusion: earth, water, fire, sky and air, this body is made of the five.

key_verses.sanskrit: प्रगट सो तनु तव आगे सोवा। जीव नित्य केहि लगि तुम्ह रोवा॥ उपजा ग्यान चरन तब लागी। लीन्हेसि परम भगति बर मागी ॥
key_verses.gist: That body lies sleeping before you, and the soul is eternal; for whom do you weep?

content_hook: The one whose arrow killed her husband was the one who sat with her and spoke about what does not die.
notes: Do not serve on day 1 of fresh grief: the 'for whom do you weep' line misleads without its scene. Use later in a grief plan, with the scene and with who is speaking.

title: Tulsidas follows his wife across a flooded river and is turned by her words
source_ref: Hagiography: Priyadas, Bhaktirasabodhini commentary on Nabhadas's Bhaktamal (1712), and the later Mool Gosain Charit attributed to Benimadhav Das (authenticity disputed). Not told in Tulsidas's own works.
the_moment: In the story the tradition tells, the young Tulsidas is so attached to his wife Ratnavali that when she goes to her father's house without him, he follows the same night, crossing a river in flood and climbing to her room. Embarrassed in front of her family, she speaks sharply.
what_they_did: She says, in the verse the tradition gives her: you have such love for this body of bone and skin; if you had the same for Shri Ram, you would have no fear of the world. He turns and leaves, and the story says he went to Prayag and then Kashi and became the poet of Ram.
the_turn: A rebuke from the person he loved most, at the moment of his greatest attachment, redirects the attachment rather than destroying it. The same intensity goes to Ram.
outcome: Tulsidas becomes a renunciant and, decades later, writes the Ramcharitmanas.
whole_arc_note: This is hagiography, told for centuries but not attested by Tulsidas himself; his own poems speak instead of an abandoned childhood and begging for scraps (see st.bhakti.tulsi_abandoned_as_a_child). The tale is usually told to praise the wife's words; it can also be read as a husband leaving a wife. Tell it as a tradition, with that ambiguity, and do not present the verse as Tulsi's.
teaching: Intense love, redirected, can become devotion; a sharp word at the right moment can turn a life.
modern_parallels: My wife said one sentence to me in anger, and it has stayed with me for ten years.
I was obsessed with a person to the point of embarrassing both of us. She told me so.
The same energy I put into chasing her, I now put into my practice.
Someone I loved told me I was living for the wrong thing, and she was right.

key_verses.gist: Such love for my body of bone and skin; had you the same for Shri Ram, you would have no fear of the world.

content_hook: A flooded river, a wife's sharp sentence, and a man who became the poet of the Ramcharitmanas. Or so the story goes.
notes: Hagiography; confidence low for historicity. The verse attributed to Ratnavali is quoted from memory and is not in the corpus. renunciation_push: the arc ends in leaving home; do not serve as advice to leave a spouse.

title: Tulsidas tells his own story: left at birth, begging for scraps
source_ref: Tulsidas, Kavitavali, Uttar Kand 57 and 72 (corpus ids tulsi_kv.7.57, tulsi_kv.7.72); Vinay Patrika 227
the_moment: In his own late poems Tulsidas looks back: my mother and father abandoned me as soon as I was born; fate wrote nothing good on my forehead. Low, scorned, timid, I craved the scraps thrown to dogs. Driven by the fire of hunger I ate morsels from every house, of every caste, as the whole world knows.
what_they_did: He heard of Ram's nature and told the Lord, just once, about his empty stomach. Ram, the master for both this world and the next, took no offence. He describes himself wandering, begging, ignored, until the Name became his support: by the grace of the Name I, a thorn bush, now bear mangoes.
the_turn: The turn is a single honest petition: baraka pet khalai, he showed his hunger once. And the Name, held as his only support.
outcome: The world now honours him like a great sage, he says, and he is amazed at it, calling himself still unlucky and not devoted enough.
whole_arc_note: Do not turn this into a rags-to-riches story. Tulsi keeps calling himself low and faulty even after the honour; the gratitude is to the Name, not to his own effort. These are his own poems, the most reliable source for his life.
teaching: Even the one whom parents and fate abandoned is taken in by the Name; asking once, honestly, is enough.
modern_parallels: I grew up without parents and ate wherever someone would feed me.
Nobody expected anything from me. Now people call me successful, and I still feel like that hungry boy.
I was adopted, and I have spent years feeling unwanted.
I once asked God for help, just once, honestly. Things changed.

key_verses.sanskrit: मातु-पिताँ जग जाइ तज्यो बिधिहूँ न लिखी कछु भाल भलाई। नीच, निरादरभाजन, कादर, कूकर-टूकन लागि ललाई॥ रामु-सुभाउ सुन्यो तुलसीं प्रभुसों कह्यो बारक पेटु खलाई। स्वारथको परमारथको रघुनाथु सो साहेबु, खोरि न लाई॥
key_verses.gist: Mother and father abandoned me as soon as I was born; fate wrote no good fortune on my brow. Low, scorned, timid, I craved dogs' scraps. Hearing of Ram's nature I told the Lord once of my empty belly; Raghunath, master of this world and the next, took no offence.

key_verses.sanskrit: जातिके, सुजातिके, कुजातिके पेटागि बस खाए टूक सबके, बिदित बात दुनीं सो। मानस-बचन-कार्य किए पाप सतिभायँ, रामको कहाइ दासु दगाबाज पुनी सो। रामनामको प्रभाउ, पाउ, महिमा, प्रतापु, तुलसी-सो जग मनिअत महामुनी-सो। अतिहीं अभागो, अनुरागत न रामपद, मूढ! एतो बडो अचिरिजु देखि-सुनी सो॥
key_verses.gist: Driven by the fire of hunger I ate morsels from everyone, high caste and low, as the world knows. Now by the power of Ram's name the world honours Tulsi like a great sage, and I marvel at it.

key_verses.sanskrit: नाम राम रावरोई हित मेरे। स्वारथ-परमारथ साथिन्ह सों भुज उठाइ कहाँ टेरे॥ १॥ जननी-जनक तज्यो जनमि, करम बिनु बिधिहु सृज्यो अवडेरे। मोहुँसो कोउ-कोउ कहत रामहि को, सो प्रसंग केहि केरे॥ २॥ फिरयौ ललात बिनु नाम उदर लगि, दुखउ दुखित मोहि हेरे। नाम-प्रसाद लहत रसाल-फल अब हौं बबुर बहेरे॥ ३॥ साधत साधु लोक-परलोकहि, सुनि गुनि जतन घनेरे। तुलसीके अवलंब नामको, एक गाँठि कइ फेरे॥ ४॥
key_verses.gist: Mother and father left me at birth; I wandered begging for my belly; now by the Name's grace I, a thorn tree, bear mangoes.

content_hook: The poet of the Ramcharitmanas wrote that his parents abandoned him at birth and he ate scraps meant for dogs.

title: Tulsidas resolves: till now I wasted my life; I will not waste it any more
source_ref: Tulsidas, Vinay Patrika 105 (corpus id tulsi_vp.105)
the_moment: Looking back on years lost to the pull of the senses, Tulsidas does not lament for long. He writes a song of waking up.
what_they_did: He declares: till now I wasted; I will not waste any more. By Ram's grace the night of worldliness is over; awake, I will not lie down in that bed again. I have found the Name, a beautiful wish-gem, and I will not let it slip from my heart's hand. I will test the gold of my mind on the touchstone of his dark form. The senses laughed at me when I was in their power; now that I am my own, I will not let them laugh again.
the_turn: Aba lon nasani, aba na nasaihon. The past is named without self-flagellation, and the resolve is given its ground: grace has ended the night; he is awake.
outcome: The song ends with the mind as a bee settling in the lotus of Ram's feet.
whole_arc_note: The resolve rests on grace (rama kripa), not willpower alone. Do not turn it into a productivity slogan; it is a devotee's waking.
teaching: What was wasted is past; by grace one wakes, and can refuse to sleep again.
framework: From VP 105: 1. name the waste plainly, once; 2. recognise that the night has ended (grace); 3. hold one thing firmly (the Name); 4. test the mind against it; 5. stop letting the senses laugh at you.
modern_parallels: I lost my twenties to scrolling and drinking. I am done.
I have wasted so many years. Today I decided not one more.
My phone was laughing at me every night. I put it in another room.
I am forty-two and I just started the thing I always said I would do.

key_verses.sanskrit: अबलों नसानी, अब न नसैहौं। राम-कृपा भव-निसा सिरानी, जागे फिरि न डसैहौं॥ १॥ पायेउँ नाम चारु चिंतामनि, उर कर तें न खसैहौं। स्यामरूप सुचि रुचिर कसौटी, चित कंचनहि कसैहौं॥ २॥ परबस जानि हँस्यो इन इंद्रिन, निज बस ह्वै न हँसैहौं। मन मधुकर पनकै तुलसी रघुपति-पद-कमल बसैहौं॥ ३॥
key_verses.gist: Till now I have wasted; I will not waste any more. By Ram's grace the night of the world is over; awake, I will not lie in that bed again. I have found the Name, a wish-gem, and will not let it fall from my heart's hand.

content_hook: 'Till now I have wasted. I will not waste any more.' Tulsidas, about 400 years ago.

title: Old Tulsidas, in unbearable pain, argues with Hanuman
source_ref: Tulsidas, Hanuman Bahuk (corpus ids tulsi_hb.21, tulsi_hb.36, tulsi_hb.38 [verse 37 in the text], tulsi_hb.42)
the_moment: Near the end of his life Tulsidas is struck by a fierce pain in his arm and body, in a Kashi swept by sickness. It does not let up day or night. He does not know whether it is time, karma, past sin or simply his constitution.
what_they_did: He writes to Hanuman, his lifelong protector, in verse after verse. He reminds Hanuman that he raised him like a child. He asks why the arm that Hanuman himself once held is now in this state. He argues, pleads, admits his own faults, and returns to trust: I live as Ram's servant and Kashi is a fine place to die; both hands hold sweets. Only, this pain is unbearable, and only Raghubir can take it away.
the_turn: Honest complaint inside trust. He does not pretend the pain is fine and does not abandon faith; he says both, loudly, to the one he trusts.
outcome: Tradition holds that the pain eased after he composed the Bahuk, and it is recited for relief from pain to this day. The poems themselves end in petition, not in a reported cure.
whole_arc_note: Keep the ambiguity of cause and the absence of a reported cure in the text itself. The value is in how he prays in pain: frank, intimate, unresolved. The cure is tradition.
teaching: In pain one may complain openly to the one we trust; complaint and trust can live in the same breath.
modern_parallels: My back pain has not let me sleep for three months, and I am angry with God.
I do not know if it is age, stress or something worse. I just want it to stop.
I keep praying and arguing in the same breath.
I am not afraid of dying. I am afraid of this pain.

key_verses.sanskrit: कालकी करालता करम कठिनाई कीधों, पापके प्रभावकी सुभाय बाय बाढरे। बेदन कुभाँति सो सही न जाति राति दिन, सोई बाँह गही जो गही समीरडावरे॥ लायो तरु तुलसी तिहारो सो निहारि बारि, सोंचिये मलीन भो तयो है तिहूँ तावरे। भूतनिकी आपनी परायेकी कृपानिधान, जानियत सबहीकी रीति राम रावरे॥३७॥ भ्ावार्थ--न जाने कालकी भयानकता है कि कर्मोकी कठिनता है, पापका प्रभाव है अथवा स्वाभाविक बातकी उन्मत्तता है। रात-दिन बुरी तरहकी पीडा हो रही है, जो सही नहीं जाती और उसी बाँहको पकडे हुए है जिसको पवनकुमारने पकडा था। तुलसीरूपी वृक्ष आपका ही लगाया हुआ है। यह तीनों तापोंकी ज्वालासे झुलसकर मुरझा गया है, इसकी ओर निहारकर कृपारूपी जलसे ...
key_verses.gist: Is it the cruelty of time, the hardness of karma, the power of sin, or my own nature gone wild? The pain is unbearable night and day; it has seized the very arm the son of the wind once held.

key_verses.sanskrit: रामगुलाम तुह हनुमान गोसाँइ सुसाँइ सदा अनुकूलो। पाल्यो हौं बाल ज्याँ आखर दू पितु मातु सों मंगल मोद समूलो॥ बाँहकी बेदन बाँहपगार पुकारत आरत आनंद भूलो। श्रीरघुबीर निवारिये पीर रहों दरबार परो लटि लूलो॥३६॥
key_verses.gist: Hanuman, servant of Ram, always kind master: you raised me like a child. Crying out in the pain of my arm, I have forgotten joy; Raghubir, remove this pain, let me lie at your court, weak and lame.

key_verses.sanskrit: जिओ जग जानकीजीवनको कहाई जन, मरिबेको बारानसी बारि सुरसरिको। तुलसीके दुहूँ हाथ मोदक है ऐसे ठाउँ, जाके जिये मुये सोच करिहेँ न लरिको॥ मोको झूठो सांचो लोग रामको कहत सब, मेरे मन मान है न हरको न हरिको। भारी पीर दुसह सरीरतें बिहाल होत, सोऊ रघुबीर बिनु सके दूर करिको॥ ४२॥
key_verses.gist: I live called the servant of Janaki's beloved; to die there is Varanasi. Both of Tulsi's hands hold sweets. But this heavy pain makes the body unbearable; only Raghubir can remove it.

content_hook: The poet who wrote the Ramcharitmanas spent his last years arguing with Hanuman about the pain in his arm.
notes: Proposed situation: health_scare_self (own illness or chronic pain); none in the current 70.

title: People call Tulsidas a rogue, a weaver, a Rajput; he does not argue
source_ref: Tulsidas, Kavitavali, Uttar Kand (corpus id tulsi_kv.7.106; the corpus text gives only the first half of the verse)
the_moment: In Kashi, the learned and the orthodox talk about Tulsidas: who is he, what caste, what is he doing writing Ram's story in the common tongue? The labels pile up.
what_they_did: He answers in one verse: call me a rogue, call me an ascetic, call me a Rajput or a weaver, whatever you like. I am not going to marry my son to anyone's daughter, and I am not going to spoil anyone's caste. The traditional second half (not in our corpus text) continues: I eat what I beg and sleep in the mosque; I have nothing to take from anyone and nothing to give.
the_turn: He refuses the contest. Their labels matter only if he needs something from them, and he does not.
outcome: He goes on writing. The work outlives every critic.
whole_arc_note: The verse is his own. The hostility of the Kashi pandits is tradition. The tone is wry, not wounded; keep it that way, and do not inflate it into defiance.
teaching: When you need nothing from your critics, their labels have nothing to hold on to.
modern_parallels: My relatives keep commenting on what I do and who I married. I have stopped explaining.
Online they call me a sellout, a fraud, an amateur. I just keep publishing.
Call me what you want. I am not asking you for anything.
I spent years trying to win over people who were never going to accept me.

key_verses.sanskrit: धूत कहौ, अवधूत कहौ, रजपूतु कहौ, जोलहा कहौ कोऊ। काहूकी बेटीसों, बेटा न ब्याहब, काहूकी जाति बिगार न सोऊ॥
key_verses.gist: Call me a rogue, call me an ascetic, call me a Rajput, call me a weaver, anyone; I will not marry my son to anyone's daughter, nor spoil anyone's caste.

content_hook: 'Call me a rogue, a weaver, whatever you like.' Tulsidas's answer to his critics fits in one line.

title: Meera refuses the life her royal family expects of her
source_ref: Meera's padas (traditionally attributed; Meera texts vary widely). Corpus: meera.kk.8 (verified). 'Mere to Giridhar Gopal' and 'Pag ghunghroo bandh' are from memory, not in corpus. Hagiography: Nabhadas, Bhaktamal; Priyadas's commentary.
the_moment: Meera, married into the royal house of Mewar, will not live as a royal widow and daughter-in-law is expected to. She sings and dances before Krishna in temples, sits with sadhus, and says openly that Giridhar is her husband. Her in-laws are outraged.
dilemma: Keep the family's honour as they define it, or keep her devotion.
what_they_did: In the padas attributed to her she says: mine is Giridhar Gopal, no one else; I have given up the family's sense of shame, what can anyone do to me? People say Meera has gone mad, my mother-in-law says I have ruined the family. The Rana sent a cup of poison, and Meera laughed as she drank it. In the corpus pada she prays: mother, father, clan and family are all after their own ends; my only true kin is Raghubar.
the_turn: The turn is the one the padas keep making: there is no second (dusro na koi). Fear of the family has nowhere to land.
outcome: Tradition says the poison turned to nectar and a snake sent in a basket became an image of Krishna; she left Mewar for Vrindavan and then Dwarka.
whole_arc_note: This is a devotee's story. It is not a lesson in individualism; what she chooses is Krishna, not herself. The poison and snake are hagiography; what her padas say directly is the social cost: called mad, called a destroyer of the family. Mark confidence honestly. Wronged stance: she is not told to adjust.
teaching: When devotion is real, the world's labels and threats lose their grip; there is no second.
modern_parallels: My in-laws say my going to the ashram shames the family.
My parents think my faith is a phase and keep trying to marry me off to fix it.
People say I have gone mad since I started singing kirtan. I have never been saner.
I chose my path and my family stopped speaking to me.

key_verses.sanskrit: तुम सुणो जी म्हारो अरजी। भवसागर में बही जात हूँ काढ़ो तो थारी मरजी। इण संसार सगो नहिं कोई सांचा सगा रघुबरजी।। मात-पिता और कुटम कबीलो सब मतलब के गरजी। मीरा की प्रभु अरजी सुण लो चरण लगावो थारी मरजी।।
key_verses.gist: Hear my plea: I am being swept along in the ocean of the world, pull me out if you will. No one in this world is truly kin; my true kin is Raghubar. Mother, father, clan and family are all after their own ends.

key_verses.ref: Meera pada, Mere to Giridhar Gopal (traditional, not in corpus)
key_verses.gist: Mine is Giridhar Gopal, no other; I have left the family's sense of shame, what can anyone do?

key_verses.ref: Meera pada, Pag ghunghroo bandh (traditional, not in corpus)
key_verses.gist: People say Meera has gone mad; my mother-in-law says I have ruined the family. The Rana sent a cup of poison; Meera laughed as she drank it.

content_hook: They called her mad. They sent her poison. She sang: mine is Giridhar Gopal, no other.
notes: Only meera.kk.8 is verified in corpus. The two famous padas are quoted from memory; Meera attributions are uncertain across editions. Poison and snake episodes are hagiography (confidence low for historicity).

title: Meera: only the wounded know the wounded
source_ref: Meera pada 'He ri main to prem diwani' (corpus id meera.kk.3, Kavitakosh popular reading)
the_moment: Meera is in the pain of separation and no one around her understands it. They think it strange, or a madness, or something to be talked out of.
what_they_did: She sings it instead: I am mad with love and no one knows my pain. Only the wounded knows the state of the wounded; only the jeweller knows the worth of the jewel. My bed is on the stake, how can I sleep? My beloved's bed is in the sky, how will we meet? Struck by pain I wander forest to forest and find no healer. Meera's pain will end only when the Dark One is the healer.
the_turn: She stops expecting the uninjured to understand and names who can heal it.
outcome: The pada ends in hope, not in arrival.
whole_arc_note: This is devotional viraha; the 'beloved' is Krishna. It speaks to anyone who is not understood in their pain, but do not flatten it into a romance or a diagnosis.
teaching: Only one who has been wounded understands the wound; the pain of longing for God is healed only by God.
modern_parallels: Nobody in my family understands why I grieve my guru this much.
People keep giving me advice. Only my friend who lost her child just sat with me.
I am tired of explaining my pain to people who have never felt it.
I feel a longing for something I cannot name, and no one gets it.

key_verses.sanskrit: हे री मैं तो प्रेम-दिवानी मेरो दरद न जाणै कोय। घायल की गति घायल जाणै, जो कोई घायल होय। जौहरि की गति जौहरी जाणै, की जिन जौहर होय। सूली ऊपर सेज हमारी, सोवण किस बिध होय। गगन मंडल पर सेज पिया की किस बिध मिलणा होय। दरद की मारी बन-बन डोलूँ बैद मिल्या नहिं कोय। मीरा की प्रभु पीर मिटेगी, जद बैद सांवरिया होय।
key_verses.gist: I am mad with love; no one knows my pain. The wounded knows the state of the wounded, the one who has been wounded. The jeweller knows the jewel. Meera's pain will go when the Dark One is the healer.

content_hook: 'Only the wounded knows what the wounded goes through.' Meera, 500 years ago.

title: Meera has found the jewel of Ram's name and wants nothing more
source_ref: Meera pada 'Payo ji maine ram ratan dhan payo' (corpus id meera.kk.13, Kavitakosh popular reading)
the_moment: After a life of losses, Meera sings of something she has gained.
what_they_did: She sings: I have found the wealth of the jewel of Ram's name. My true guru gave me this priceless thing and, in his grace, made me his own. I have found the capital of many lives and lost everything else in the world. It does not run out when spent, thieves cannot steal it, it grows a quarter more every day. With truth as the boat and the true guru as boatman, I have crossed the ocean.
the_turn: Nothing to turn: this is gratitude spoken from fullness.
outcome: She sings Giridhar's glory with joy.
whole_arc_note: Use this for people who are grateful or content; it should never be framed as a fix for a problem. It is the voice of someone who already has what she wants.
teaching: The wealth that grows when spent and cannot be stolen is the Name, received by grace.
modern_parallels: I have nothing new to ask for. I just want to say thank you.
My guru gave me a mantra twenty years ago and it has only grown.
Everything I have lost has made this feel more precious.
I feel rich in a way I cannot explain to my accountant.

key_verses.sanskrit: पायो जी म्हें तो राम रतन धन पायो। वस्तु अमोलक दी म्हारे सतगुरू, किरपा कर अपनायो॥ जनम-जनम की पूँजी पाई, जग में सभी खोवायो। खरच न खूटै चोर न लूटै, दिन-दिन बढ़त सवायो॥ सत की नाँव खेवटिया सतगुरू, भवसागर तर आयो। 'मीरा' के प्रभु गिरिधर नागर, हरख-हरख जस पायो॥
key_verses.gist: I have found the wealth of the jewel of Ram's name. My true guru gave me this priceless thing. It does not run out when spent, no thief can steal it, it grows a quarter more each day.

content_hook: 'Spending does not exhaust it, thieves cannot take it, it grows every day.' Meera on the one wealth she cared about.

title: Surdas: I have danced enough, Gopal
source_ref: Surdas, Vinay pada 'Ab main nachyo bahut Gopal' (corpus id sur.vp.200, Sursagar vinay padas, Gita Press OCR)
the_moment: Surdas looks at his whole life as one long performance on a stage, dressed and made up by his own cravings.
what_they_did: He sings: I have danced a great deal, Gopal. I wore the costume of lust and anger, a garland of sense objects round my neck. The anklets of delusion jingled, the sweet sound of praise and blame, the mind deluded was the drum, playing out of time. Craving sang inside, beating many rhythms; I tied the sash of maya at my waist and put the mark of greed on my forehead. I showed millions of skills, not knowing water from land or time. Nandlal, take away all of Surdas's ignorance.
the_turn: The image itself is the turn: seeing the whole drive of a life as a costume and a dance makes it possible to ask to stop.
outcome: The pada ends in a single petition, not a claimed liberation.
whole_arc_note: The weariness is real and honest; it is not depression and should not be served as such. It is the devotee's turning from performing to asking.
teaching: Seen clearly, the life driven by craving is a costume dance; one can ask to stop.
modern_parallels: I have performed my whole career. I am tired of the costume.
Fifty years of chasing approval and the next thing. I want to stop dancing.
Every promotion was another set of anklets.
I looked at my life and saw a show I did not want to be in anymore.

key_verses.sanskrit: अब में नाच्यों बहुत गुपाल ! काम-कफ्रोध को पहिरि चोलना, कंठ बिषय की माल ॥ महामोह के नृूपुर बाजत, निंदा सब्द रखाल। भ्रम-सोयो मन भयो पखावज, चलत अखसंगत चाल ॥ तृष्ना नाद करति घट भीतर, नाना विधि दे ताल । माया कौ कटि फेंटा बाँध्यो, लोभ-तिलक दियो भाल ॥ कोटिंक कला काछि दिखराई, जल-थल सुधि नहिें काल। सूरदास की सब अविद्या दूरि करो नेंदलाल ॥
key_verses.gist: I have danced a great deal, Gopal, wearing the costume of lust and anger, a garland of sense objects at my throat; the anklets of delusion ring, praise and blame make the sweet sound; Nandlal, take away all of Surdas's ignorance.

content_hook: 'I have danced enough, Gopal.' Surdas's resignation letter from the show.

title: Surdas sings only of his own sins until his guru tells him to sing of Krishna
source_ref: Surdas's vinay padas (corpus sur.vp.195, sur.vp.271, verified). The meeting with Vallabhacharya is from the Chaurasi Vaishnavan ki Varta (hagiography; from memory).
the_moment: Surdas, a singer at Gau Ghat near Mathura, sings mostly of how sinful he is: who is as crooked, wicked and lustful as me? I forgot the one who gave me this body, I am a traitor to my salt, I run after the senses like a village pig.
what_they_did: In the poems he begs: Lord, do not hold my faults in mind. Your name is 'the one who sees all equally'. One piece of iron is kept in worship, another lies in a butcher's house; the philosopher's stone does not distinguish, it turns both into gold. One stream is called a river, another a drain of dirty water; when they meet the Ganga, both become Ganga.
the_turn: In the Varta account, Vallabhacharya hears him and says: you are Sur (a hero, and his name), why do you whine like this? Sing something of the Lord's lila. He initiates him, and Surdas begins the Krishna lila padas of the Sursagar.
outcome: Surdas becomes the great singer of Krishna's childhood and love, one of the eight poets of the Pushti tradition.
whole_arc_note: The self-reproach padas are his own and are not wrong; the tradition does not throw them away. The Vallabha turn is hagiography and should be told as such. The pairing is the point: honest confession, then the instruction to stop dwelling and sing of what is good.
teaching: Confession has its place; then stop wailing and sing of the One who turns iron to gold.
modern_parallels: I have spent years in therapy talking about what is wrong with me. My teacher told me to start talking about what I love.
Every prayer I say is a list of my failures.
I keep apologising. My mentor said: enough, now do the work you love.
I was sure I was too dirty to be forgiven. Then someone told me the Ganga does not check.

key_verses.sanskrit: मो सम कौन कुटिल खल कामी। तुम सो कहा छिपी करुनामय, सब के अंतरजामी ! ॥ जो तन दियो, ताहि बिसरायो, ऐसौो नोन-हरामी। भरि भरें उदर बिपे को धावत, जैसे खूकर ग्रामी ॥ सखुनि सतसंग होत जिय आलस, विपयिनि सँग विसरामी । भ्रीहरि-चरन छाड़े विमुखनि की निसि-दिन करत गुल्ठामी ॥ पापी परम, अधम, अपराधी, सब पतितनि में नामी। खरदास प्रभु अथम-उधारन खुनिये श्रीपति खामी॥
key_verses.gist: Who is as crooked, wicked and lustful as me? What is hidden from you, compassionate one, knower of all hearts? I forgot the one who gave me this body.

key_verses.sanskrit: हमारे प्रभु, ओगुन चित न घरो । समदरसी है नाम तुम्हारा, सोई पार करौ॥ इक लोहा पूजा में राखत, इक घर वधिक परो। सो दुविधा पारस नहि जानत, कंचन करत खरो॥ इक नदिया इक नार कहावत, मैलो नीर भरौ। जब मिलि गए तब एक-बरन हे, गंगा नाम परौ॥ तन माया, ज्यौ ब्रह्म कहावत, खूर सु मिलि बिगरौ। के इनकौ निरधार कीजिये, के प्रन जात ठरौ॥
key_verses.gist: Lord, do not hold my faults in mind; your name is the one who sees all as equal. One iron is kept in worship, one lies in a butcher's house; the philosopher's stone knows no difference and makes both pure gold.

content_hook: Surdas kept singing 'who is as wicked as me'. His guru said: you are Sur, stop whining and sing of Krishna.
notes: Padas verified in corpus (OCR text, some noise). The Vallabhacharya episode is from the Chaurasi Vaishnavan ki Varta; quoted from memory; confidence medium as tradition, low as history.

title: Krishna, now a prince in Mathura, sends word home: no one here calls me Kanhaiya
source_ref: Surdas, Bhramargeet padas 'Pathik sandeso kahiyo jaay' and 'Nike rahiyo Jasumati maiya' (corpus ids sur.bgs.9, sur.bgs.10, ed. Ramchandra Shukla)
the_moment: Krishna has left Gokul for Mathura. He has killed Kamsa, is honoured as a prince, and everything is splendid. He finds a traveller going toward Braj and gives him a message for the woman who raised him.
what_they_did: Tell mother not to worry; we two brothers will come in four or five days. Since the day I left you, no one has called me Kanhaiya. I have never had breakfast in the morning or warm milk in the evening. Keep my flute safe, and do not let Radha steal any of my toys. Tell Nanda baba I was very cruel to leave. Though Mathura has great splendour, nothing pleases me without you; meeting people from Braj cools my heart.
the_turn: The great one names exactly what he misses: being called by his childhood name, the small daily care. He sends love and reassurance, and admits his fault in leaving.
outcome: In the Bhramargeet, the promised return does not come quickly; Braj waits, and the gopis' longing becomes the subject of Uddhav's mission.
whole_arc_note: Do not tidy the ending: 'four or five days' becomes a long absence. The tenderness of the message and the pain of the delay both belong to the scene.
teaching: Splendour abroad cannot replace being known by your childhood name at home.
modern_parallels: I moved to Bangalore for the job. Nobody here calls me by my pet name.
I have a good life in Toronto, but no one makes chai the way my mother did.
I keep telling my mother I will visit next month.
I sent my mother a voice note: I am fine, do not worry. I cried after.

key_verses.sanskrit: पथिक! सँदेसो कहियो जाय। आवैंगे हम दोनों भैया, मैया जनि अकुलाय॥ याको बिलगु बहुत हम मान्यो जो कहि पठयो धाय। कहँ लौं कीर्ति मानिए तुम्हरी बड़ो कियो पय प्याय॥ कहियो जाय नंदबाबा सों, अरु गहि पकर्‌यो पाय। दोऊ दुखी होन नहिं पावहिं धूमरि धौरी गाय॥ यद्यपि मथुरा बिभव बहुत है तुम बिनु कछु न सुहाय। सूरदास ब्रजबासी लोगनि भेंटत हृदय जुड़ाय॥९॥
key_verses.gist: Traveller, take a message: we two brothers will come, mother, do not be anxious. Though Mathura has great splendour, without you nothing pleases me; meeting Braj people cools my heart.

key_verses.sanskrit: नीके रहियो जसुमति मैया। आवैंगे दिन चारि पाँच में हम हलधर दोउ भैया॥ जा दिन तें हम तुमतें बिछुरे काहु न कह्यो 'कन्हैया'। कबहूँ प्रात न कियो कलेवा, साँझ न पीन्हीं धैया॥ बंसी बेनु सँभारि राखियो और अबेर सबेरो। मति लै जाय चुराय राधिका कछुक खिलौनो मेरो॥ कहियो जाय नंदबाबा सों निपट निठुर जिय कीन्हो। सूर स्याम पहुँचाय मधुपुरी बहुरि सँदेस न लीन्हो॥१०॥
key_verses.gist: Stay well, mother Yashoda; we will come in four or five days. Since the day I parted from you, no one has called me Kanhaiya; I have had no breakfast in the morning, no warm milk at dusk.

content_hook: Krishna, prince of Mathura, sent word home: since I left, no one has called me Kanhaiya.

title: The elephant king fights the crocodile with all his strength, and calls only when it is gone
source_ref: Surdas, Vinay pada 'Bharoso nam ko bhari' (corpus id sur.vp.241); story from Bhagavata Purana 8.2 to 8.4
the_moment: An elephant king, bathing with his herd, is seized by a crocodile. He pulls with all his strength, his herd pulls with him, and it goes on for a very long time. The herd gives up and leaves. The strength runs out.
what_they_did: Surdas compresses it to one line: when the crocodile surrounded the elephant king, his strength was lost; defeated, he called out, and Giridhari came.
the_turn: The call comes only when every other resource is gone: hari ke jab teri dinhi. Surdas then turns it on himself: you came for him, for Sudama, Draupadi, Vibhishan, Dhruva; why are you so slow for me?
outcome: In the Bhagavata, Hari comes at once, leaving his mount behind, and frees him.
whole_arc_note: Do not moralise this as 'should have called sooner'. The text honours the struggle and the call; Surdas adds his own impatience to it. For a secular reader, it is about asking for help when your own strength is finished.
teaching: When your own strength is spent, call; help comes to the one who calls with nothing left.
modern_parallels: I tried to handle my depression on my own for two years. Last week I finally called someone.
My whole family was pulling with me, and then even they let go.
I did not ask for help until I was completely out of options.
Why is help so slow for me, when it came so quickly for others?

key_verses.sanskrit: भरोसो नाम को भारी । प्रेम सो ज्ञिन नाम लीन्हों, भए अधिकारी ॥ ग्राह जब गजराज घेरथों, बल गयौ हारी। हारि के जब टेरि दीन्ही, पहुँचे गिरिधारी ॥ सुदामा-दारिद भंजे, . कूबरी तारी। द्रॉपपी को चीर बढ़यो, दुसासन गारी ॥ विभीषन को लंक दीनी, रावनहि मारी। दास धुव कों अटल पद दियौो, राम-दरबारी ॥ सत्य भक्तहि तारिबे को लीला बिस्तारी। बेर मेरि क्‍यों ढील कीन्ही, सुर बलिहारी ॥
key_verses.gist: Great is trust in the Name. When the crocodile surrounded the elephant king, his strength was lost; defeated, he called out, and Giridhari came. Why the delay for me? says Sur.

content_hook: The elephant fought with everything he had. Only when it was all gone did he call. Surdas asks: why are you slower for me?
notes: Corpus text is OCR from the Gita Press 1955 edition; noise in the Devanagari.

title: Kabir goes looking for a bad person and finds himself
source_ref: Kabir dohas (corpus kabir.kk.146 from Kavita-Kaumudi; kabir.kkdv.421 from a popular compilation)
the_moment: Kabir, a weaver in Kashi who spoke plainly about everyone's hypocrisy, Hindu and Muslim alike, turns the same eye on himself.
what_they_did: He says: I went out looking for the bad one, and found no one bad. When I searched my own heart, there was no one as bad as me. And elsewhere: keep your critic close, build him a hut in your courtyard; without water or soap he cleans your nature.
the_turn: The search outward turns inward. The critic becomes a cleaner rather than an enemy.
outcome: The dohas give no outcome; they are the turn itself.
whole_arc_note: This is not self-hatred: Kabir's voice is wry and clear-eyed. And it is not advice to keep abusers close; nindak here is the one who points out your faults. Kabir's life is mostly legend; these dohas are popular readings, attributed with medium confidence.
teaching: Look for fault in your own heart first; keep the one who criticises you close.
modern_parallels: I was making a list of everyone who had wronged me, and I noticed I was the common factor.
My colleague criticises everything I do. I have started to see that half of it is right.
I spent a week judging my brother-in-law and then caught myself doing the same thing.
I want the friend who tells me the truth, not the one who agrees.

key_verses.sanskrit: बुरा जो देखन मैं चला बुरा न मिलिया कोय। जो दिल खोजौं आपना मुझसा बुरा न कोय॥१४६॥
key_verses.gist: I went to look for the bad one; no bad one did I find. When I searched my own heart, no one was as bad as me.

key_verses.sanskrit: निंदक नियारे राखिये, आंगन कुटि छबाय । / बिन पाणी बिन सबुना, निरमल करै सुभाय ॥ 421 ॥
key_verses.gist: Keep the critic near; build him a hut in your courtyard. Without water, without soap, he cleans your nature.

content_hook: Kabir went looking for the bad person. Then he looked in the mirror.

title: Kabir the weaver: the body is a fine sheet, to be returned unstained
source_ref: Kabir pada 'Jhini jhini bini chadariya' (traditional, not in corpus). Supporting dohas in corpus: kabir.kk.23 (the clay and the potter), kabir.kk.19 (do tomorrow's work today).
the_moment: Kabir earns his living at a loom. He sings about what he knows: thread, warp, weft and cloth.
what_they_did: In the famous pada he sings of the body as a finely woven sheet, made over months with the eight-petalled lotus as the spinning wheel and the five elements and three gunas as thread. Gods, sages and men have all worn it and stained it. Das Kabir wore it with great care and laid it down just as it was. In his dohas the clay tells the potter: why do you trample me? A day will come when I will trample you. And: what you would do tomorrow, do today; what today, do now; in a moment the world ends, when will you do it then?
the_turn: The image of the returned sheet makes mortality practical: the question is not how long the cloth lasts but how it is kept.
outcome: The pada ends with the sheet returned unstained.
whole_arc_note: The chadariya pada is quoted from memory and not verified here; the dohas are verified. Kabir's biography (weaver, Kashi, Niru and Nima, Ramanand) is tradition with low historical confidence.
teaching: The body is lent cloth: wear it carefully, do your work now, and give it back clean.
modern_parallels: My father just died and I keep asking what it means to live well with the time I have.
I keep putting off the important things for tomorrow.
I am a craftsman. Kabir's sheet made me cry.
I want to give it back clean. That is all I want now.

key_verses.ref: Kabir pada, Jhini jhini bini chadariya (traditional, not in corpus)
key_verses.gist: Finely, finely woven is the sheet. Gods, sages and men all wore it and stained it; Das Kabir wore it with care and laid it down just as it was.

key_verses.sanskrit: माटी कहै कुम्हार को तू क्या रूँदै मोहिं। इक दिन ऐसा होइगा मैं रूँदूँगी तोहि॥२३॥
key_verses.gist: The clay says to the potter: why do you trample me? A day will come when I will trample you.

key_verses.sanskrit: काल करै सो आज कर आज करैं सो अब्ब। पलमें परलै होयगी बहुरि करैगा कब्ब॥१९॥
key_verses.gist: What you would do tomorrow, do today; what today, do now. In a moment the end will come; when will you do it then?

content_hook: A weaver's last word: wear the body like borrowed cloth, and give it back clean.

title: Kabir to his own restless mind: slowly, slowly
source_ref: Kabir doha 'Dhire dhire re mana' (corpus id kabir.kkdv.12, popular compilation)
the_moment: The mind wants the result now. Kabir talks to it the way a gardener would.
what_they_did: He says: slowly, slowly, O mind; everything happens slowly. The gardener may pour a hundred pots of water; the fruit comes when its season comes.
the_turn: The gardener does water; the doha does not say stop working. It says the timing of the fruit is not in the pot.
outcome: No outcome is given; the season will decide.
whole_arc_note: Keep the hundred pots: the teaching is effort without forcing the season, not passivity.
teaching: Water faithfully; the fruit comes in its season, not because you poured more.
modern_parallels: I have applied to a hundred jobs this year. I am trying to believe the season will come.
We have been trying for a baby for three years.
My startup is doing everything right and still growing slowly.
I water my practice every day and nothing seems to change.

key_verses.sanskrit: धीरे-धीरे रे मना, धीरे सब कुछ होय । / माली सींचे सौ घड़ा, ॠतु आए फल होय ॥ 12 ॥
key_verses.gist: Slowly, slowly, O mind; everything happens slowly. The gardener pours a hundred pots; the fruit comes when the season comes.

content_hook: The gardener can pour a hundred pots of water. The mango still waits for its season.

title: Rahim, once the empire's great general, writes about the turning of days
source_ref: Rahim's dohe (corpus rahim.169, rahim.26, rahim.58, rahim.37). Biography of Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan (Akbar's commander; fall from favour under Jahangir) from memory.
the_moment: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan was one of the most powerful men of Akbar's empire: commander, scholar, famously generous. Under Jahangir he fell out of favour; history records that he lost sons and position. In his dohas the man who had everything writes about losing it.
what_they_did: He writes: Rahim, sit quiet and watch the turning of the days; when good days come, it will not take long to set things right. Kin are many while wealth lasts; adversity is the touchstone, and those who pass it are true friends. Do not go to anyone's door and regret it; everyone comes for your wealth, adversity takes them all away. And: in Chitrakoot dwells the king of Avadh; whoever falls on hard times comes to this land.
the_turn: He does not fight the turn of fortune; he waits it out, and he learns who his friends were. The last doha sends the fallen to the place where Ram himself lived in exile.
outcome: The dohas give no reported recovery; tradition says he lived his last years in reduced circumstances.
whole_arc_note: The biography is history from memory and should be told lightly. The dohas are his own (Wikisource text). 'Sit quiet' here is about not panicking or begging during a downturn; it is not advice to a wronged person to accept injustice.
teaching: Fortune turns; in the bad days stay quiet, learn who your friends are, and go where the exiled go.
modern_parallels: I was the VP everyone wanted to know. After the layoff, my phone stopped ringing.
My business collapsed and I learnt in one month who my real friends were.
I am trying not to beg or panic. I am waiting for the days to turn.
We lost the family money. My father says the good days will come back.

key_verses.sanskrit: रहिमन चुप ह्वै बैठिए, देखि दिनन को फेर। / जब नीके दिन आइहैं, बनत न लगि है देर॥१६९॥
key_verses.gist: Rahim, sit quiet and watch the turning of the days; when good days come, it will not take long to put things right.

key_verses.sanskrit: कहि रहीम सम्पति सगे, बनत बहुत बहु रीति। / बिपति कसौटी जे कसे, तेई साँचे मीत॥२६॥
key_verses.gist: In wealth, says Rahim, many become kin in many ways; adversity is the touchstone, and those who pass it are true friends.

key_verses.sanskrit: कोउ रहीम जनि काहु के, द्वार गए पछिताय। / सम्पति के सब जात हैं, बिपति सबै लै जाय॥३७॥
key_verses.gist: Let no one go to another's door and regret it, Rahim; all come for wealth, and adversity takes them all away.

key_verses.sanskrit: चित्रकूट में रमि रहे, रहिमन अवध नरेस। / जेहि पर बिपदा परत है, सो आवत यहि देस॥५८॥
key_verses.gist: In Chitrakoot dwells the king of Avadh, Rahim; whoever is struck by adversity comes to this land.

content_hook: The man who commanded Akbar's armies wrote: sit quiet, and watch the days turn.

title: Rahim gives with his eyes lowered, and explains why
source_ref: Rahim doha 'Denhar kou aur hai' (corpus id rahim.95, verified). The question attributed to Tulsidas is tradition, from memory.
the_moment: Rahim, as Khan-i-Khanan, was known for giving to anyone who came, and for doing it with his eyes cast down.
what_they_did: The tradition says someone, often named as Tulsidas, asked him in verse: where did you learn this way of giving, Nawab? The higher your hand rises, the lower your eyes fall. Rahim answered: the Giver is someone else, who sends it day and night; people mistake it for me, so my eyes are lowered.
the_turn: He refuses the role of benefactor. He is the hand, not the giver.
outcome: The answer has outlived both men as a line on how to give.
whole_arc_note: Rahim's reply is verified in the corpus; the question and its attribution to Tulsidas are tradition with low confidence. Keep it light.
teaching: When you give, remember who the Giver is; that is why the eyes go down.
modern_parallels: People keep thanking me for the scholarship fund. It is my late father's money, really.
I donate every month and I feel awkward when anyone praises me.
I got credit for a team win and I wanted to look at the floor.
My grandmother always gave food without looking at the person's face, so they would not feel small.

key_verses.sanskrit: देनहार कोउ और है, भेजत सो दिन-रैन। / लोग भरम हम पै धरैं, याते नीचे नैन॥९५॥
key_verses.gist: The Giver is someone else, who sends it day and night; people put the illusion on me, and so my eyes are lowered.

content_hook: 'Why do you lower your eyes when you give?' 'Because people think I am the giver.'
